items.prompt: How many independent boolean features can be represented directly by a w-bit mask when each feature owns one bit?

feedback.reason: One bit stores one independent true-or-false feature.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Assigning one independent feature to each position creates w boolean coordinates. Each coordinate has two values, so the word can encode `2 × 2 × … × 2 = 2^w` different combined states, but it still names only w independent features. State count and feature capacity are different quantities.

items.prompt: A state mask uses bit i to mean resource i is acquired. Which expression tests whether resource i is acquired?

options.text: (state AND (1 shifted left by i)) is nonzero.
(state OR (1 shifted left by i)) is nonzero.
state shifted left by i is nonzero.

feedback.reason: A one-hot mask extracts the selected membership bit.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The one-hot mask `1 << i` contains a one only at position i. AND evaluates each position independently: every unrelated position meets zero and disappears, while position i remains nonzero only if state also contains a one there. The result therefore tests membership without altering state.

items.prompt: Which operation combines two feature masks into a state containing every feature present in either mask?

feedback.reason: OR represents set union over boolean feature positions.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

At one feature position, OR has the union truth table: `0|0=0`, while `0|1`, `1|0`, and `1|1` all equal one. Applying that rule independently at every position keeps exactly the features present in the left mask, the right mask, or both.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.addition: If both masks contain the same bit, arithmetic addition carries into a neighboring position and corrupts feature membership.

items.prompt: Which operation produces a mask containing only features present in both state masks?

feedback.reason: AND is set intersection over one-bit feature memberships.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

At each feature position, AND yields one only for `1&1`; every case containing a zero yields zero. The output therefore includes exactly the memberships shared by both masks and excludes features present on only one side.

items.prompt: A transition releases every resource selected by mask released. Which update matches the contract?

options.text: state = state AND complement(released), using the declared width.

feedback.reason: Release requires selected membership bits to become zero while all others remain unchanged.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Within the declared width, `~released` has zero at every selected release position and one elsewhere. AND with state therefore forces released positions to zero (`x&0=0`) while copying every unselected state bit (`x&1=x`). This is set difference `state \ released`.

items.prompt: When do two bitmask-encoded boolean states represent exactly the same feature set?

options.text: When their masks are bitwise equal.
When they contain the same number of set bits.
When their highest set bit matches.

feedback.reason: The bit-position mapping is a canonical state representation.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

With one stable feature-to-position mapping, a feature set determines one unique bit pattern. Two sets are equal exactly when every position agrees, which is ordinary mask equality. Equal popcount or one shared high bit constrains only part of the pattern and permits different memberships.

items.prompt: Which expression tests whether feature sets a and b are disjoint?

feedback.reason: Any shared feature would survive the AND.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

AND computes the intersection one position at a time. If any feature is present in both masks, that position contributes a one and the result is nonzero; conversely, a zero result proves that no position has membership one on both sides.

items.prompt: Which expression tests whether every feature in mask a is also present in mask b?

feedback.reason: Intersecting a with b should preserve all of a when a is a subset of b.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

AND extracts from a only positions also present in b. If every feature of a is contained in b, no one from a is removed and `a & b == a`; if even one is missing, that position becomes zero and the equality fails.

items.prompt: A task requires all flags in required to be enabled in state, while additional flags are allowed. Which test is correct?

feedback.reason: The test extracts required positions and verifies that every one is present.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

`state & required` clears every position not requested and retains only required positions that state actually contains. Equality with `required` proves none are missing. Extra state flags are masked out before comparison and therefore remain allowed.

items.prompt: A system needs 70 independent boolean features, but the chosen primitive mask exposes only 64 usable bits. What is the correct design response?

options.text: Use a wider arbitrary-precision or multiword representation, or another explicit state structure.
Map multiple unrelated features to the same bit.
Shift a 64-bit one by positions 64 through 69 and assume portability.

feedback.reason: One-bit-per-feature encoding requires at least as many usable positions as features.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

An injective one-bit mapping for 70 features needs at least 70 usable positions. A 64-bit word cannot supply positions 64–69; reusing positions makes distinct states collide, and oversized shifts cannot create storage outside the word. The canonical fix is a wider integer, multiple words, or another explicit structure.

items.prompt: Which problem states are natural candidates for one-bit-per-feature encoding? Select all that apply.

options.text: Which members of a small fixed universe have been visited.
Which small indexed resources are currently used.
An arbitrary unbounded count for every feature.

feedback.reason: Bitmask state is suitable for bounded collections of independent booleans.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

One-bit-per-feature encoding fits questions of membership over a small declared universe: visited or not, enabled or not, used or not. Each feature must have only two independent states. An unbounded count has more than two values and cannot be recovered from a single membership bit.

items.prompt: Which set-style operations are represented correctly by bitwise operators? Select all that apply.

feedback.reason: Boolean membership algebra maps directly to OR, AND, and XOR.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Evaluate one membership position. OR is one when either set contains the feature, matching union; AND is one only when both contain it, matching intersection; XOR is one only when exactly one contains it, matching symmetric difference. Difference requires `a & ~b`, not arithmetic addition.

items.prompt: Which requirements make a bit-position mapping reliable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Each feature has one unique bit position.
The mapping remains stable anywhere masks are compared or persisted.
The available width and valid positions are documented.
Feature labels must be sorted numerically.

feedback.reason: The mask is only canonical when every position has one stable meaning inside a declared width.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Uniqueness prevents two features from colliding in one position. Stability ensures a stored or transmitted mask has the same meaning everywhere it is compared. Documented width defines valid positions, complement behavior, and capacity. Numerical label order is merely an authoring convenience.

items.prompt: Which transitions preserve unselected feature bits? Select all that apply.

options.text: Set selected features with state OR mask.
Clear selected features with state AND complement(mask).
Toggle selected features with state XOR mask.
Replace state with state AND mask.

feedback.reason: A state transition should alter only positions explicitly selected by the transition mask.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

For any unselected position the transition mask contains zero. OR gives `stateBit|0 = stateBit`, AND with complemented mask gives `stateBit&1 = stateBit`, and XOR gives `stateBit^0 = stateBit`; all preserve it. Direct `state & mask` instead meets unselected positions with zero and clears them.

items.prompt: Which tests are important for bitmask state representation? Select all that apply.

options.text: The zero mask with no features enabled.
Two different features enabled separately and together.

feedback.reason: State tests should cover empty, full, and independence properties.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The zero mask tests the identity and absence boundary. The full usable mask exercises the highest position, capacity, and width-limited complement. Enabling two features separately and together proves that their positions are independent and do not collide. One middle bit covers none of those boundaries.

items.prompt: Arrange the design process for a bitmask state model.

elements.text: List the boolean features that must be represented.
Assign one unique zero-based bit position to each feature.
Choose a representation wide enough for every assigned position.
Document membership meaning and legal state operations.

feedback.reason: Representation design begins with semantic fields and ends with an explicit positional contract.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The semantic universe must be known before storage is selected. Only after every independent boolean is listed can positions be assigned injectively and the highest position determine required width. Documentation then makes encoded masks comparable and persistent across components.

items: List the exact independent boolean features and exclude fields that require counts or larger values.
Assign each listed feature one unique, stable zero-based position.
Choose a fixed, multiword, or arbitrary-width representation that includes the highest assigned position.
Document position meanings, width, valid states, persistence rules, and supported transitions.

blocks.text: For an ordering task, define the feature mapping before encoding or transforming a mask. Otherwise a numerically correct word can still mean the wrong state.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for encoding a selected feature collection into one mask.

elements.text: Look up each selected feature's assigned bit position.
OR the corresponding one-hot mask into state.
Test that all selected features are present and no unintended positions were used.

feedback.reason: Encoding accumulates independent feature memberships with OR.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Zero is the empty-set identity. For each selected feature, the stable mapping supplies i and `1 << i` supplies its singleton set; OR accumulates those memberships without clearing earlier ones. Verification ensures no collision, overflow, or unintended position entered the mask.

items: Initialize the state to the all-zero empty mask.
Resolve each selected feature through the canonical feature-to-position mapping.
Create its one-hot mask and OR it into the accumulated state.
Verify every selected membership is present, no unselected bit is set, and all positions fit the declared width.

items.prompt: Arrange a transition that acquires features add, releases features remove, and then verifies required features.

elements.text: Update state = state AND complement(remove) within the width.
Check that the extracted bits equal required.

feedback.reason: Set and clear transitions update distinct selected positions, after which the required-state postcondition is tested.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

OR first forces every `add` position to one. Width-limited AND NOT then forces every `remove` position to zero while preserving others, so removal wins on overlap under this stated policy. Only the completed state can be intersected with `required` and compared with `required` to prove the postcondition.

items: Apply `state = state | add` to acquire every selected feature.
Apply `state = state & ~remove` within the declared width to release selected features.
Compute `presentRequired = state & required` on the final state.
Verify `presentRequired == required`; document a different add/remove precedence if removal should not win on overlap.

items.prompt: On one fixed-width machine word, a state transition performs a constant number of OR, AND, XOR, and comparison operations. Select time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: The feature count fits inside the fixed word.

feedback.reason: A constant number of primitive fixed-word operations is constant time.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Under the fixed-word machine model, OR, AND, XOR, and comparison each process one word in O(1). A constant number of those primitives therefore totals O(1) time, and retaining a constant number of masks uses O(1) auxiliary words. If features span a growing number of words, this model no longer applies.

items: Count primitive operations: the transition performs a fixed number independent of input size.
Count retained words: state and constant-many masks coexist.
State the boundary: both O(1) claims require every feature to fit the declared fixed-width word.

items.prompt: A dynamic-programming table stores one constant-size value for every state of n independent boolean features. Select initialization time and table space.
constraints: Every one of the 2^n masks receives one table entry.

feedback.reason: A compact encoding of one state does not make the full state space small.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Each of n independent features has two values, so there are 2^n distinct masks. Initializing one constant-size table cell for each mask performs 2^n writes and stores 2^n values, giving O(2^n) initialization time and O(2^n) table space even if an individual mask fits one word.

items: Count states by multiplying two choices for each independent feature: `2 × … × 2 = 2^n`.
Charge one initialization operation per table entry to obtain Θ(2^n) time.
Charge one constant-size stored value per mask to obtain Θ(2^n) table space.
